Abstract
Executing vision-language models (VLMs) aboard low-Earth
orbit satellites enables flexible processing of observation data
without first downlinking it to the ground. On commercial
off-the-shelf payloads, however, a request may span mul-
tiple execution windows: power and thermal constraints,
fault-triggered reboots, and competing payload demands
can interrupt inference before it completes. Each shutdown
discards volatile activations and KV caches, forcing an un-
protected request to repeat work after restart.
We present OrbitWeaver, a framework that preserves VLM
inference progress across onboard interruptions through
coordinated checkpointing and recovery. Its phase-aware
checkpointing selects recovery boundaries according to the
state lifetimes and computational characteristics of vision
encoding, language-model prefill, and decoding, balancing
storage traffic against recomputation. Its dependency-aware
dynamic recovery schedules restoration from partially com-
pleted states across the layer and token-chunk dimensions.
By overlapping checkpoint and weight reads with recom-
putation, it reduces restart latency; the recovery planner
computes an optimal execution order under its scheduling
model within 100 ms.
Experiments on satellite payload hardware using on-orbit
telemetry traces show up to a 4.07× end-to-end speedup
and a 3.56× reduction in SSD write volume over the eval-
uated baselines. A 72-hour deployment on two low-Earth
orbit satellites demonstrates that OrbitWeaver retains infer-
ence progress and resumes execution across repeated bus-
enforced shutdowns.
∗Corresponding author.
1
Introduction
Low-Earth orbit (LEO) satellites are emerging as powerful
platforms for satellite computing [14], a new paradigm that
shifts heavy data processing directly to orbit to overcome the
intolerable latency of the traditional bent-pipe architecture.
Backed by the integration of commercial off-the-shelf (COTS)
edge hardware (e.g., NVIDIA GPUs on Starcloud-1 [59]), this
high-performance orbital infrastructure is now physically
accessible and cost-effective [2, 20, 70]. Leveraging these
advanced platforms, Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are
rapidly becoming the premier workload for dynamic space
missions. Instead of relying on fragmented, task-specific
models, VLMs offer unified, on-the-fly functional elastic-
ity for effortless mission redirection [33, 65, 77]. Pioneering
space-agency initiatives, such as NASA’s Prithvi geospa-
tial foundation model and the European Space Agency’s
(ESA) Phi-Sat-2 mission, have recently validated the feasibil-
ity of executing such foundation models directly in orbit [17],
marking the dawn of intelligent satellite computing.
Mismatch: sustained VLM execution vs. bus-enforced
interruptions. On-orbit VLM inference requires sustained
computation, while spacecraft-level control can interrupt
payload execution before a request completes.
Long-running on-orbit VLM workloads. VLM inference on
satellites can involve high-resolution images or multiple im-
ages within a single request. These inputs can produce long
visual-token sequences, increasing the computation needed
to complete the request. For example, Earth observation (EO)
workloads can involve processing image sequences of up to
30 frames [15] and images reaching 44.93 megapixels [45].
Our in-orbit evaluation of Qwen3-VL 2B on Sat-1 and Sat-
1
arXiv:2610.29183v1  [cs.DC]  21 Oct 2026

Huang et al.
2 shows that a typical 3-minute mission processes only 8
frames (> 32𝐾tokens).
Short and unpredictable inference survival windows. On-
board computing payloads face unpredictable interruptions
that severely truncate execution windows. These abrupt halts
primarily stem from three sources: (i) Bus-enforced hard shut-
downs due to dynamic power constraints or thermal viola-
tions [9]. For example, VLM inference on Sat-1 and Sat-21
spikes the payload temperature from 45◦C to 55◦C in just
48 s, leading to sudden thermal cutoffs that vary drastically
depending on the satellite’s orbital state. (ii) On-orbit anom-
alies (e.g., radiation-induced SEUs or software faults) that
trigger the Fault Detection, Isolation, and Recovery (FDIR)
system. FDIR forces sudden system reboots to clear errors;
our private LEO satellite telemetry data reveals that in worst-
case scenarios, such reboots occur as frequently as once per
minute [19]. (iii) Resource contention from intermittent, high-
priority payloads (e.g., bursty transceivers or laser transmit-
ters) that preempt shared bus resources [22].
To tackle this mismatch, we propose OrbitWeaver, an effi-
cient and reliable VLM inference engine designed for satel-
lite computing. OrbitWeaver achieves transparent, minimal-
overhead preservation of VLM execution progress by dynam-
ically checkpointing essential states to onboard non-volatile
storage (e.g., eMMC/SSD). Upon rebooting, it swiftly recon-
structs the context to resume inference. Achieving this goal
requires addressing two challenges:
• Checkpointing phase: fast checkpointing vs. efficient recov-
ery. Preserving execution progress creates a dilemma: mini-
mizing checkpointing I/O for active inference speed versus
maximizing progress preservation for rapid recovery. Fine-
grained checkpointing (e.g., per-token/layer) captures com-
plete progress but incurs substantial I/O overheads, whereas
coarse-grained checkpointing (e.g., per-chunk) minimizes
I/O but forces expensive recomputation of discarded intra-
chunk states. This trade-off manifests across all VLM phases.
For instance, in memory-bound decoding, saving per-token
KV caches and hidden states ensures optimal recovery at
prohibitive costs (>100%), while merely saving token IDs
eliminates I/O but forces full KV cache recomputation from
scratch, introducing a latency of > 50 seconds.
• Recovery phase: unavoidable weight-checkpoint I/O in un-
structured resumption. Unlike traditional LLM context switch-
ing with uniform states (e.g., full prompt KV caches), ar-
bitrary orbital bus-enforced interruptions leave an irregu-
lar, “staircase-like” inference progress state. Resuming from
this unstructured state complicates masking the coupled I/O
overhead of reloading static weights alongside dynamic KV
caches and hidden states from disparate positions. Specifi-
cally, loading a layer’s weights unlocks computation across
multiple chunks, whereas loading its KV cache only enables
that specific chunk. With numerous valid starting points
1We refer to the two satellites as Sat-1 and Sat-2 throughout this paper.
along this irregular boundary, finding the optimal execution
sequence to maximize compute-I/O overlap under complex
dependency constraints becomes a highly non-trivial sched-
uling challenge.
To solve these challenges, OrbitWeaver incorporates two
key techniques:
• Phase-aware checkpointing. To resolve the checkpoint-
ing dilemma, OrbitWeaver leverages the heterogeneous lifes-
pans of VLM states (persistent KV caches vs. transient hid-
den states) and phase-specific bottlenecks to establish adap-
tive recovery boundaries: (i) Vision encoding (layer bound-
ary): Because bidirectional self-attention couples all image
patches, patch chunks cannot be finalized independently.
OrbitWeaver therefore persists the full-patch hidden state
after each vision layer, using layer boundaries as recovery
points. (ii) LLM prefill (2D block boundary): Because prefill is
compute-bound, checkpointing both KV Cache and hidden
states minimally impacts active inference. To mitigate SSD
wear-out, OrbitWeaver groups operations into 2D blocks (ex-
ecution grids spanning multiple sequence chunks and model
layers), checkpointing transient hidden states exclusively at
block boundaries. (iii) LLM decoding (multi-token boundary):
Decoding is memory-bound, making per-token checkpoint-
ing prohibitively expensive. Recognizing that the decoding
recovery bottleneck is massive weight-loading I/O rather
than lightweight recomputation, OrbitWeaver aggregates KV
cache updates across multi-token boundaries. This amortizes
flash write overhead, as the slight recomputation increase is
completely masked by the inevitable weight-loading I/O.
• Dependency-aware dynamic recovery. To mitigate
coupled I/O bottlenecks during unstructured resumption,
we observe that despite recovery computation heavily out-
weighing I/O latency, strict dependencies still cause severe
I/O stalls. To maximize compute-I/O overlap, OrbitWeaver
unlocks dependencies multi-dimensionally: (i) 2D block-first
recovery: Rigid layer- or chunk-first strategies only resolve
single-dimension dependencies. Instead, executing a 2D
block immediately unlocks both horizontal (chunk) and ver-
tical (layer) dependencies, triggering a computation cascade
to mask concurrent SSD reads. (ii) Optimal scheduling plan:
Selecting the optimal ready block to minimize recovery la-
tency is critical, as each choice unlocks distinct downstream
computation cascades to maximize I/O masking; yet this
scheduling is NP-hard. We dramatically prune this search
space via two domain-specific properties: (a) deferring hidden
state loads to retain DRAM activations and avoid redundant
SSD reads, and (b) packing layer-wise I/O to coalesce weight
reads into coarse-grained streams. This enables OrbitWeaver
to mathematically solve the optimal execution order within
100 ms.
We implemented OrbitWeaver atop transformers [67]
and evaluated it on hardware testbeds mirroring two real
satellite computing payloads: the NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX
(16 GB) and AGX Orin (64 GB). These represent the onboard

platforms of Sat-1 and Sat-2. Our evaluations are driven by
five interruption traces: four derived from telemetry col-
lected on Sat-1 and Sat-2, and one from the Dellingr satel-
lite [28]. Using these scenarios, we run advanced edge-viable
VLMs, including Qwen3-VL 2B/4B/8B and MiniCPM-V 4.5,
on remote sensing QA datasets. Compared to three state-of-
the-art baselines (two variants of a representative intermit-
tent DNN execution runtime and a conventional KV cache
context-saving approach), OrbitWeaver achieves up to a
4.07× end-to-end speedup. Furthermore, it reduces check-
pointing and recovery latency by up to 61.9% and 85.6%, re-
spectively, while slashing SSD write volume by up to 3.56×.
To the best of our knowledge, we are the first academic
work to successfully deploy and sustain VLM inference
directly in orbit. We deployed OrbitWeaver on Sat-1
and Sat-2 for a 72-hour in-situ earth observation case
study. The deployment demonstrates that OrbitWeaver
preserves progress and sustains VLM inference across
repeated bus-enforced shutdowns.
Our contributions are summarized as follows:
• We are the first to identify the bottleneck of bus-enforced
shutdowns in on-satellite VLM inference.
• We propose OrbitWeaver, the first efficient and reliable
VLM inference system for satellite computing by intro-
ducing efficient checkpointing and recovery.
• We implement OrbitWeaver and deploy it on Sat-1 and
Sat-2. Our evaluation shows that OrbitWeaver achieves
up to a 4.07× end-to-end speedup, while a 72-hour in-
orbit deployment demonstrates sustained VLM inference
across repeated bus-enforced shutdowns.
2
Background
2.1
On-Satellite Vision-Language Models
Satellite computing shifts data processing and services
directly to orbit. This approach overcomes the severe com-
munication bottlenecks of the traditional bent-pipe architec-
ture, where limited downlink bandwidth and brief contact
windows make downlinking raw data for ground-side pro-
cessing intolerably slow for modern space missions [14].
This orbital computing capability is enabled by moving be-
yond traditional radiation-hardened controllers and inte-
grating commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) computing plat-
forms—such as CPUs, GPUs, and FPGAs—into modern satel-
lites [13, 26, 57, 70]. Consequently, satellites are evolving
from simple data collectors into orbital edge nodes capable
of executing diverse tasks. Early examples include onboard
filtering to discard cloudy images (Phi-Sat-1 [26]) or select
high-value samples (Kodan [13]). More recently, platforms
like Starcloud-1 are pushing hardware boundaries by carry-
ing data-center-class NVIDIA H100 GPUs in orbit, demon-
strating that high-performance AI accelerators can now be
deployed as standard satellite payloads.
As shown in Figure 1, a typical satellite computing plat-
form consists of a computing payload and a spacecraft bus
that supports, monitors, and controls the payload. The pay-
load runs a VLM inference engine on top of an operating
system, using SSD for persistent storage, RAM for volatile
memory, and CPUs and GPUs for computation. During in-
ference, the engine loads model weights and input data from
SSD into RAM and dispatches tensor operations to the proces-
sors, while intermediate tensors and runtime states remain
in volatile memory. Meanwhile, the spacecraft bus supplies
payload power through the electrical power system (EPS),
monitors payload temperature through sensors, and man-
ages communication and fault protection through TT&C
and the onboard computer (OBC) with FDIR. These bus sub-
systems communicate over a CAN bus and can disconnect
payload power or trigger a reboot when power, thermal, or
safety constraints require intervention, abruptly interrupting
the ongoing inference.
Vision-Language Models for LEO satellites. With ad-
vanced hardware in orbit, satellite computing tasks are
rapidly shifting toward VLMs. For critical applications like
Earth observation (EO), traditional fragmented, task-specific
models are being replaced by VLMs, which offer a “one-
for-all”, prompt-driven framework that provides functional
elasticity for dynamic missions without retraining over-
head [17]. Furthermore, driven by the massive expansion
of LEO constellations, initiatives like Starcloud [21] are
actively constructing “space data centers” to deliver real-
time, space-native VLM inference and token generation
services directly to users. Robust, sustained VLM execution
is therefore essential for next-generation LEO systems.
On-satellite VLM inference pipeline. A VLM is a multi-
modal model that converts images and text instructions into
text outputs by combining visual encoding with language-
model generation. As illustrated in Figure 2, after the on-
board camera captures an image, the acquired visual data
is fed into the VLM for inference, initiating a three-phase
pipeline. In the first phase (vision encoding), a Vision Trans-
former partitions the input image into patches and encodes
them into visual tokens [16]. During the second phase (LLM
prefill), the model processes these visual tokens alongside the
prompt tokens, establishing the attention state and initial-

izing the Key-Value (KV) cache for the multimodal context.
Finally, in the LLM decoding phase, the language model gen-
erates the response autoregressively, producing one token
at a time while continuously utilizing and updating the KV
cache established during the prefill phase. These phases in-
volve different intermediate states, including visual tokens,
prefill states, KV cache, and partial outputs.
2.2
Bus-enforced Shutdowns in On-Satellite VLM
Inference
Onboard computing payloads operate under strict spacecraft-
wide power and safety constraints. The spacecraft bus can
abruptly disconnect payload power to preserve essential
functions or protect hardware, regardless of the inference
software’s status [19, 50]. We term these platform-initiated
interruptions bus-enforced shutdowns, which can terminate
VLM requests unpredictably. They primarily stem from three
sources:
• Dynamic power and thermal constraints. The electri-
cal power system (EPS) autonomously sheds non-essential
loads (e.g., computing payloads) when demand exceeds sup-
ply [4, 50]. This power availability fluctuates with solar illu-
mination and battery aging, which alters discharge curves
over time and makes supply highly non-linear. Furthermore,
thermal limits force sudden shutdowns. As shown in Fig-
ure 2, VLM inference on Sat-1 spikes the payload enclosure
temperature from 45◦C to the 55◦C threshold in just 48 s,
triggering an immediate power-off. Driven by external or-
bital states, these shutdowns are entirely decoupled from
VLM execution boundaries (e.g., prefill and decoding steps).
• Hardware/software anomalies and FDIR interven-
tions. The harsh space environment introduces stochastic
anomalies, such as radiation-induced Single-Event Upsets
(SEUs) or software faults (e.g., erroneously activating Sun-
pointing during an eclipse). The onboard Fault Detection,
Isolation, and Recovery (FDIR) system continuously moni-
tors payload health. Upon detecting these anomalies or hard-
ware violations (e.g., overcurrent) [19], FDIR forces sudden
system reboots to clear errors. These fault-protection actions
occur randomly, completely ignoring any payload execution
schedule. Our private LEO satellite telemetry data reveals
worst-case scenarios where these unpredictable reboots oc-
cur once per minute.
• Resource contention from intermittent payloads. The
computing payload shares the bus with high-priority, in-
termittent payloads (e.g., bursty transceivers) [22]. Their
unpredictable activation—driven by ground station visibil-
ity or mission commands—aggressively consumes limited
power and thermal budgets, often preempting the comput-
ing payload [4, 22]. Together, these stochastic factors render
payload shutdown timing and duration highly erratic and
not practical to profile offline.
On-satellite VLM inference needs fast checkpointing
and recovery. As illustrated in Figure 2, bus-enforced shut-
downs can terminate any inference phase and discard its
in-memory states, including ViT/LLM hidden states and the
KV cache. Restoring power alone therefore cannot resume
execution; recovery requires checkpoints persisted in non-
volatile storage. Consequently, VLM inference requires low-
overhead checkpointing and rapid recovery without advance
knowledge of shutdown timing. Our scope addresses execu-
tion interruption and volatile state loss, assuming persistent
weights and checkpoints in non-volatile storage remain in-
tact (leaving radiation-induced persistent storage corruption
to orthogonal hardware research).

3
Design Overview
We present OrbitWeaver, an efficient and reliable VLM infer-
ence system designed for COTS satellites. Figure 3 shows the
overview of OrbitWeaver. To address the progress-loss prob-
lem caused by bus-enforced shutdowns, OrbitWeaver adopts
checkpointing and recovery to make VLM inference resum-
able across power-off and reset events. During inference,
OrbitWeaver persists selected boundary states from volatile
memory to SSD; after a shutdown, it validates and reloads
the latest checkpoint to reconstruct the execution context
and continue the unfinished request instead of restarting
from scratch.
However, making checkpointing and recovery efficient on
COTS satellites is nontrivial. Checkpointing must preserve
enough state to resume each VLM phase, but excessive per-
sistence increases SSD traffic, energy use, and normal-path
latency. Recovery must reload model weights and check-
pointed states from SSD, but a poor recovery order exposes
I/O stalls and leaves little useful computation time within
each short execution window. To address these two chal-
lenges, OrbitWeaver introduces two techniques.
Efficient checkpointing. OrbitWeaver defines phase-aware
recoverable units that preserve only the states needed for re-
sumption while bounding runtime checkpoint overhead. For
LLM prefill, OrbitWeaver uses block-wise checkpointing over
token chunks and layer groups, avoiding the hidden-state
write cost of layer-wise checkpointing and the recomputa-
tion cost of chunk-wise checkpointing. For vision encoding,
OrbitWeaver checkpoints layer-boundary hidden states be-
cause bidirectional attention makes patch chunks invalid
recovery units. For decoding, OrbitWeaver batches KV cache
checkpoints across generated tokens to avoid excessive small
writes. OrbitWeaver further uses phase-specific storage lay-
outs to reduce I/O interference, avoid unnecessary recovery
reads, and ensure crash-consistent checkpoint persistence.
Dynamic recovery. OrbitWeaver reduces recovery latency
by scheduling SSD reads and block computation over the
checkpointed frontier. Instead of following a fixed chunk-
first or layer-first order, OrbitWeaver restores the states that
unlock useful computation and overlaps later SSD reads
with dependency-ready blocks. By exploiting the regular
dependency structure of VLM prefill, OrbitWeaver reduces

4
Efficient Checkpointing
OrbitWeaver preserves VLM progress across satellite shut-
downs by persisting intermediate states at checkpoint bound-
aries. Each boundary must expose enough state for correct
resumption while limiting SSD traffic, energy cost, and run-
time overhead. We identify three primary issues:
• VLM phases expose different state dependencies, so a uni-
form checkpoint boundary cannot efficiently support vi-
sion encoding, prefill, and decoding;
• Checkpoint granularity creates a recomputation–write
trade-off: persisting more states reduces replay after shut-
downs, but increases checkpoint writes during normal
execution.
• Checkpoint persistence must be storage-aware: frag-
mented writes increase runtime overhead and SSD wear,
while storing hidden states and KV tensors in an in-
terleaved layout forces recovery to read unnecessary
data.
To address these issues, OrbitWeaver designs phase-aware
recoverable units. It uses block-wise checkpointing for prefill
(§4.1), phase-specific checkpointing for vision and decoding
(§4.2), and an SSD layout that supports efficient and crash-
consistent checkpoint persistence (§4.3).
4.1
Block-wise Prefill Checkpointing
When prefill completes without a shutdown, preserving its
KV cache is sufficient for the later decoding phase. However,
a satellite reset may occur in the middle of prefill, discarding
all in-memory progress before the final KV cache is pro-
duced. Therefore, OrbitWeaver must checkpoint prefill at
finer granularity, along its layer and token dimensions. This
leads to two straightforward checkpoint placements.
Naïve solution: Layer-wise checkpointing. A natural de-
sign is to follow the LLM’s layer-by-layer execution order
and place a checkpoint boundary after each layer, as shown
in Figure 4(a). However, this layer-level granularity comes at

Figure 5. Storage–recomputation trade-off of different
checkpointing granularities.
a high checkpointing cost. Since recovery from a layer bound-
ary requires the input to the next layer, OrbitWeaver must
persist the full-sequence hidden state at every layer bound-
ary, whose size scales with the multimodal input length,
including both visual tokens and prompt tokens. As shown
in Figure 5, layer-wise checkpointing minimizes lost progress
but requires the largest checkpoint storage: about 14.34 GiB
for Qwen3-VL 2B and 27.65 GiB for MiniCPM-V 4.5.
Naïve solution: Chunk-wise checkpointing. Another de-
sign is to partition the input sequence into fixed-size chunks
and place a checkpoint boundary after each chunk completes
all 𝐿layers, as shown in Figure 4(b). This reduces checkpoint
traffic: after a chunk finishes all layers, the checkpoint only
needs to preserve the KV tensors produced by the chunk,
rather than full-sequence hidden states after every layer. As
shown in Figure 5, chunk-wise checkpointing keeps storage
near the total KV size, but incurs the highest recomputation
overhead: about 14.34 × 103 and 18.43 × 103 token-layers for
Qwen3-VL 2B and MiniCPM-V 4.5, respectively.
The comparison above reveals a structural property of
LLM prefill: KV tensors are long-lived context; once pro-
duced, they are reused by later chunks and by decoding.
Hidden states are short-lived boundary states; they are
only needed to feed the next layer group after recovery.
Layer-wise checkpointing over-preserves hidden states,
while chunk-wise checkpointing under-preserves them
and cannot resume inside a chunk. OrbitWeaver exploits
this separation by maintaining a minimal recovery fron-
tier: it accumulates KV tensors for completed computation
and materializes hidden states only at sparse layer-group
boundaries.
OrbitWeaver design: Block-wise checkpointing. Based
on this frontier view, OrbitWeaver partitions prefill along
both the token and layer dimensions. It splits the input
sequence into chunks of 𝐶tokens and groups the 𝐿LLM
layers into groups of 𝐺consecutive layers, forming a two-
dimensional grid of recoverable units (Figure 4(c)). Each unit
computes 𝐺layers over 𝐶tokens. When a unit completes,
OrbitWeaver persists the KV tensors produced by the unit
and the hidden states at the output boundary of the layer
group.
This design preserves only the states needed at the re-
covery frontier. Compared with layer-wise checkpointing,
it avoids persisting full-sequence hidden states after every
layer. Compared with chunk-wise checkpointing, it can re-
sume inside a chunk and replay at most the unfinished 𝐺×𝐶
unit instead of the entire chunk across all 𝐿layers. The
choice of 𝐺and 𝐶determines where OrbitWeaver operates
on the storage–recomputation trade-off. Smaller units re-
duce recomputation after a reset but increase transfer, write,
and metadata overhead; larger units reduce checkpointing
overhead but lose more computation after a shutdown. Or-
bitWeaver selects 𝐺and 𝐶through lightweight offline cali-
bration on the LRS-VQA [45] for each model-device pair. The
calibration profiles a small set of candidate configurations on
representative prefill inputs and selects the one that satisfies
a user-defined checkpoint overhead budget while bounding
the replay cost after a reset. With 𝐺= 4, OrbitWeaver re-
duces lost progress to about 2.04 × 103 token-layers for both
models, with checkpoint sizes of 8.96 GiB for Qwen3-VL 2B
and 13.82 GiB for MiniCPM-V 4.5 (Figure 5).
4.2
Checkpointing Vision and Decode
Beyond LLM prefill, the other VLM phases expose different
recovery boundaries. Vision encoding is dominated by layer-
by-layer bidirectional attention, while decoding advances
autoregressively one token at a time. OrbitWeaver there-
fore uses phase-specific checkpointing policies for these two
phases.
Layer-wise vision checkpointing. Unlike LLM prefill,
whose causal attention allows completed token chunks to be
finalized independently, vision encoding uses bidirectional
self-attention over all patches [16]. Since each patch output
depends on the full patch sequence, patch chunks cannot
serve as valid recovery units. Once a vision layer completes,
its full-patch hidden state becomes the complete input to
the next layer, so OrbitWeaver checkpoints vision encoding
at layer boundaries by persisting this state.
Batched decode checkpointing. Decoding advances au-
toregressively, generating one output token at a time. Each
generated token appends new entries to the KV cache, and
future tokens depend on these entries. Therefore, decoding
only checkpoints the KV cache as its recoverable progress
state, while hidden states are transient within each decode
step and need not be persisted. Checkpointing after every to-
ken minimizes replay but is inefficient: each token adds only
a small KV slice, so per-token checkpoints cause frequent
device-to-host transfers and fragmented SSD writes. This is
especially costly for memory-bound decoding [80], where
extra checkpoint writes compete with incremental KV cache
access. OrbitWeaver therefore batches decode checkpoints.
It accumulates the KV slices for 𝐷generated tokens and
persists them as one checkpoint unit, together with the gen-
erated token IDs and the current decode position. If a reset
occurs between two decode checkpoints, recovery reloads
the latest persisted KV cache and replays at most 𝐷decode
steps.

4.3
I/O-Efficient Storage Layout
The checkpointing policies above define logical recoverable
units; OrbitWeaver then lays out their persisted states ac-
cording to each phase’s access pattern to reduce I/O overhead
and ensure crash consistency.
Prefill layout. This layout is optimized for the asymmetric
access patterns of checkpointing and recovery. For block-
wise prefill checkpoints, OrbitWeaver stores the states pro-
duced at each completed block boundary as one contiguous
record (Figure 6(a)), which turns each checkpoint into a se-
quential write. Each record separates boundary hidden states
from the block’s multi-layer KV tensors: the former resumes
the next layer group, while the latter serves later chunks
and decoding. This separation lets recovery restore only the
needed hidden-state or KV region, avoiding unnecessary
I/O. OrbitWeaver further stores KV tensors in layer-major
order, allowing a layer’s prefix KV to be restored through
sequential reads.
Vision layout. For vision checkpoints, OrbitWeaver reduces
storage overhead by persisting only the layer-boundary hid-
den states (Figure 6(b)). Each hidden-state checkpoint is writ-
ten as one contiguous record. To tolerate resets during check-
point writes, OrbitWeaver alternates between two aligned
buffers: the new buffer is marked valid only after its write
completes, while the previous buffer remains valid during
the write. If a reset interrupts the current write, recovery
selects the newest complete buffer.
Decode layout. Decode checkpoints must handle a dynam-
ically growing output sequence (Figure 6(c)). Since future
token length is unknown, OrbitWeaver uses an append-only
layout instead of preallocating fixed regions for layers or
positions. Each decode checkpoint appends the KV slices
generated by one decode batch as a single record. Within
the record, keys from all layers are written contiguously, fol-

lowed by values from all layers, turning batched KV updates
into sequential writes. This layout grows naturally with gen-
eration while preserving efficient checkpoint persistence.
Checksum and crash consistency. System resets can
happen during checkpoint writes, leaving partially written
checkpoint data on storage. To handle this, OrbitWeaver
appends a checksum-protected commit footer to each check-
point record. The footer contains the record length, check-
point index, and payload checksum, and the record is
considered committed only after this footer is durably
written.
5
Dynamic Recovery
After the satellite recovers from a shutdown, the VLM in-
ference must restore the checkpointed state from the SSD
and resume computation. The latency of this process greatly
affects the end-to-end completion time of a request.
Fast recovery is critical. To motivate the need for fast
recovery, we run a controlled experiment with Qwen3-VL
2B/4B/8B on Jetson AGX Orin and Jetson Orin NX. The work-
load is a 64K-token remote-sensing VQA request constructed
from our evaluation datasets. We fix the checkpointed ex-
ecution progress and reset pattern, and vary the recovery
time paid at the beginning of each execution window. Figure
7 shows that increasing recovery time from 5 s to 25 s raises
end-to-end completion time by up to 5.04× and 5.56× on AGX
and Orin, respectively. Therefore, OrbitWeaver minimizes
exposed recovery I/O before computation resumes.
In this section, we first show why fixed recovery orders
create avoidable I/O stalls (§5.1). Then we formulate recovery
as an I/O–computation scheduling problem (§5.2). Finally, we
illustrate the algorithm to find the optimal schedule (§5.3).
5.1
Dependency-Aware Recovery
Following the execution order of existing LLM prefill imple-
mentations, the most direct recovery strategy is to replay
the remaining prefill blocks in the same static order. The
order of existing implementations is typically chunk-first or
layer-first. However, recovery optimizes a different objective
from normal inference: it must load weights and checkpoints
and start computation as early as possible. To minimize re-
covery latency, we need to minimize exposed I/O, i.e., the
time computation stalls waiting for unfinished reads.

Figure 8. Fixed recovery orders expose avoidable I/O stalls.
• Chunk-first static recovery. In Figure 8(a), the first chunk
has completed before the shutdown. A chunk-first order
resumes from (𝐿1,𝐶2) and proceeds to (𝐿2,𝐶2). This switch
requires 𝑊2 and 𝐾𝑉2,1; any part of these reads not hidden
by the computation of (𝐿1,𝐶2) becomes exposed I/O. Thus,
chunk-first recovery can stall when it switches to a higher
layer before the required layer state has finished loading.
• Layer-first static recovery. In Figure 8(c), layer 𝐿1 has
completed through chunk 𝐶2 before the shutdown. A layer-
first order starts with (𝐿1,𝐶3), which requires𝑊1, 𝐾𝑉1,1, and
𝐾𝑉1,2 before any computation can run, exposing them at the
beginning of recovery. Thus, layer-first recovery can stall by
choosing a block whose inputs are not yet available, even
when other blocks are ready to execute.
• Ideal dependency-aware recovery. Ideally, we can avoid
these stalls by following data readiness rather than a fixed
order. In Figure 8(b), recovery keeps computing ready blocks
in 𝐿1 to hide the reads needed by 𝐿2. In Figure 8(d), recovery
first executes the ready prefix of 𝐿2 to hide the reads needed
later by (𝐿1,𝐶3) ((𝐿2,𝐶3) must wait for (𝐿1,𝐶3)). The ideal re-
covery order therefore depends on which weights, KV cache,
and hidden states are available, motivating a constrained
I/O–computation scheduling problem.
5.2
Recovery as a Scheduling Problem
To realize dependency-aware recovery, OrbitWeaver formu-
lates recovery as a scheduling problem over I/O and compute
tasks to maximize I/O-compute overlap.
Task definition. Let 𝑁and 𝐿be the total number of chunks
and layers after layer grouping (§4.1), respectively. There are
four types of tasks as summarized in Table 1. LLM’s causal
attention requires each block to depend on: (i) earlier blocks
in the same layer; (ii) the same block from the previous layer.
Thus, any computed block implies all blocks left and below
it in the prefill grid are already computed. Intuitively, the
completed blocks form a staircase frontier in the prefill grid,
as shown by the pink polyline in Figure 9(a). Formally, let
𝑓𝑖denote the number of completed blocks in layer 𝑖, with

Problem formulation. With the dependencies between
tasks, recovery becomes a constrained I/O–computation
scheduling problem. Let I be all the load tasks (i.e., W𝑖, H𝑖,𝑗,
and K𝑖,𝑗), C be all the compute tasks (i.e., C𝑖,𝑗), and T = I∪C
be the set of all tasks. A recovery schedule is equivalent to
assigning each task 𝑥∈T a start time 𝑠(𝑥). Let 𝜏𝑥be the

task 𝑥occupies the interval 𝐽𝑥= (𝑠(𝑥),𝑠(𝑥) + 𝜏𝑥). A valid
schedule must satisfy three conditions: (i) each task starts
after its predecessors finish; (ii) I/O tasks do not overlap; and
(iii) compute tasks do not overlap:

5.3
Optimal Recovery Plan
The optimization problem above is an instance of precedence-
constrained two-machine scheduling. The general case of
this problem is NP-hard. Our problem size is |T | = 𝑂(𝑁𝐿),
where 𝑁grows with the request input length, so an algo-
rithm exponential in |T | is unacceptable.
Fortunately, VLM prefill has a regular dependency struc-
ture that allows us to develop a specialized algorithm. We
find three opportunities to reduce the computing complexity:
• Deferring loading hidden states. First, each check-
pointed hidden state H𝑖,𝑗is used only by the block directly
above it, C𝑖+1,𝑗. Therefore, OrbitWeaver can defer loading
H𝑖,𝑗until C𝑖+1,𝑗starts and pack this read into the compute
task.
• Greedily scheduling compute tasks. Second, once the
order of I/O tasks is fixed, any work-conserving order of
ready compute tasks yields the same exposed I/O, so the
compute side can schedule them greedily. With each hidden-
state read packed into its corresponding compute task, each
packed compute task hides 𝜏C −𝜏H of I/O.
• Packing I/O of the same layer. Third, because no com-
pute task in a layer can start before the layer weights and all
preceding KV blocks are loaded, delaying these reads until
immediately before the last one does not worsen the sched-
ule. By repeatedly applying this operation, the I/O tasks of
the layer can be made consecutive, with arbitrary internal
order. So we pack𝑊𝑖and all 𝐾𝑖,𝑗in layer 𝑖into a single layer
I/O operation, whose I/O cost is denoted by 𝜌𝑖.
Given these properties, we reduce the original 𝑂(𝑁𝐿)
block-level recovery problem to choosing an order for 𝑂(𝐿)
layer I/O operations. Each loaded layer incurs I/O time but
unlocks compute tasks that can mask later I/O. We model this
process by growing the loaded set from 𝑆0 = ∅: if layer 𝜋𝑚is
loaded at step 𝑚, then 𝑆𝑚= 𝑆𝑚−1 ∪{𝜋𝑚} for 1 ≤𝑚≤𝐿; let
𝑅(𝑆) be the total I/O time spent on layers in 𝑆and 𝐶(𝑆) the
total compute time they make available. The total exposed
I/O is
𝐸(𝜋) = max
1≤𝑚≤𝐿(𝑅(𝑆𝑚) −𝐶(𝑆𝑚−1))+ ,
(4)
where (𝑥)+ = max(𝑥, 0).
Finding the optimal layer order. Eq. (4) shows that once
the current loaded set 𝑆𝑚is fixed, all future loading costs and
decisions depend only on 𝑆𝑚, regardless of the specific layer
order used to reach it. Therefore, we can use subset dynamic
programming to find the optimal layer loading order. Let
𝐹[𝑆] be the minimum exposed I/O achievable after exactly
the layers in set 𝑆have been loaded. We have:



𝑖∈𝑆
𝑆′=𝑆\{𝑖}
max {𝐹[𝑆′], 𝑅(𝑆) −𝐶(𝑆′)}
∀𝑆≠∅,
𝐹[∅] = 0.
(5)
OrbitWeaver enumerates loaded sets 𝑆by increasing car-
dinality, records the best predecessor for each transition, and
backtracks to obtain the optimal layer order. The algorithm
uses 𝑂(2𝐿) space and 𝑂(𝐿· 2𝐿) time for 𝐿layers; for Qwen3-
VL 8B, it finishes within 100 ms when the layer group size
𝐺≥2.
6
Implementation
We implement OrbitWeaver with 9,617 lines of Python and
1,741 lines of CUDA/C++ on top of transformers. The pro-
totype processes one request at a time on a single GPU,
matching our satellite payload setting. OrbitWeaver is not
tied to transformers: its checkpointing and recovery mech-
anisms operate on VLM execution states and can be inte-
grated into engines such as vLLM [34] and SGLang [79].
Context compression. During long decoding phases, re-
peated resets may force recovery to reload the full prefill KV
context many times. OrbitWeaver therefore optionally com-
presses the persisted KV cache after prefill and stores it in a
packed layout for decode recovery, reducing decode-stage
recovery latency by up to 5.02×. Our prototype supports
KIVI [43] and TurboQuant [73], and can run KV cache quan-
tization asynchronously without blocking decoding.
Checksumming and crash consistency. To tolerate re-
sets during checkpoint writes, OrbitWeaver protects each
checkpoint record with a checksum-protected commit footer.
The footer is written atomically using pwritev2() on an
O_DIRECT file, aligned to the NVMe AWUPF [51] of the satel-
lite SSD. After fdatasync(), recovery accepts only records
with a valid footer and matching checksum, discarding in-
complete or corrupted records.
7
Evaluation
7.1
Experiment setup
Hardware setup. We test OrbitWeaver on two NVIDIA Jet-
sons with different compute capabilities: Jetson Orin NX
(8-core ARM CPU, 1.9 TFLOPS Ampere GPU, 16 GB mem-
ory) and Jetson AGX Orin (12-core ARM CPU, 5.3 TFLOPS
Ampere GPU, 64 GB memory), mirroring the computing pay-
loads of Sat-1 and Sat-2. Both devices run Linux for Tegra
R36.4.3.
Models and dataset. We conduct experiments using four
typical edge-sized VLMs: Qwen3-VL 2B/4B/8B and MiniCPM-
V 4.5 (8B). All models run W4A16 inference using GPTQ
quantization and Marlin kernels. We use LRS-VQA [45] as
a representative remote-sensing VQA workload; its images
have an average resolution of 7,099×6,329 pixels. To evaluate
checkpointing and recovery performance, we construct VLM

requests with specified lengths using image and text inputs

Baselines. We compare OrbitWeaver with 4 baselines, in-
cluding a naive no-checkpoint implementation, two variants
of SONIC [27] that targets general DNN inference on in-
termittent systems, and HCache that targets datacenter
LLM context recovery. Since SONIC does not support GPU
and HCache does not open-source their code, we reim-
plement their techniques as described in their papers on
transformers framework.
• No checkpoint: naive VLM inference without checkpoint-
ing or recovery.
• SONIC-layer [27]: layer-grained checkpointing that
saves both KV cache and hidden states.
• SONIC-chunk [27]: chunk-grained checkpointing that
saves KV cache during chunk-first prefill.
• HCache [25]: hidden-state checkpointing with append-
based storage and KV reconstruction during recovery.
Metrics. We mainly measure the end-to-end inference du-
ration, recovery latency, inference latency, total SSD write
amount, device level write amplification (DLWA), and energy
consumption. We obtain DLWA by collecting I/O traces at
runtime and replaying them in MQSim [63]. Energy is mea-
sured with tegrastats. Before measuring recovery latency,
we clear the OS page cache to evaluate cold-cache recovery
performance.
7.2
End-to-end performance
We first compare the end-to-end performance of OrbitWeaver
with SONIC-layer, SONIC-chunk, and HCache under Traces
A–E (Table 2). We use interruption traces derived from
telemetry collected on Sat-1 and Sat-2, together with a trace
from Dellingr [28]. Table 2 summarizes their execution
windows.
On Orin, we evaluate Qwen3-VL 2B/4B. On AGX, we eval-
uate Qwen3-VL 2B/4B/8B and MiniCPM-V 4.5. We use a
32K-token context on Orin and a 64K-token context on AGX
(representative of the visual contexts for LRS-VQA images),
with each request generating 64 tokens during decoding.
Part of each context is occupied by image tokens, and the
rest is filled with text tokens. For each model-device pair,
we replay each trace and measure the time required to com-
plete a VLM request across interruptions. At each shutdown,
we terminate the inference process and clear its volatile
state; inference resumes from the latest checkpoint in the
next execution window. We repeat each trace until the re-
quest completes or reaches a limit of 20 full replays, after
which it is marked as incomplete. Figure 10 shows the result-
ing completion times. OrbitWeaver completes every evalu-
ated request and achieves the lowest end-to-end completion
time. For completed baseline runs, OrbitWeaver achieves
speedups of up to 4.07×, 2.89×, and 2.67× over SONIC-layer,
SONIC-chunk, and HCache, respectively. The corresponding
geometric-mean speedups are 2.95×, 1.98×, and 1.65×.
OrbitWeaver reduces both checkpointing and recovery
overhead. SONIC-layer writes KV cache and full-sequence
hidden states at layer boundaries, while SONIC-chunk re-
duces these writes but may replay an unfinished chunk
after a shutdown. HCache checkpoints hidden states and
later reconstructs the KV cache, overlapping reconstruction
with state reads. OrbitWeaver’s phase-aware checkpointing
(§4) uses block boundaries to avoid per-layer full-sequence
hidden-state writes while bounding lost work within a chunk.
During recovery, the SONIC variants reload model weights
and accumulated KV state before resuming prefill, while
HCache restores the saved context through state loading
and KV reconstruction. OrbitWeaver’s dynamic recovery
(§5) overlaps dependency-ready prefill blocks with other
reads, reducing exposed I/O and reaching the next check-
point sooner.
Crosses in Figure 10 mark requests incomplete after 20
trace replays. In the short windows of Traces A and B, recov-
ery cannot finish in time to resume useful computation. Each
shutdown interrupts recovery, forcing the next window to

restart from the same checkpoint without progress. In Trace
A, only OrbitWeaver completes Qwen3-VL 4B on Orin and
MiniCPM-V 4.5 on AGX; in Trace B, the SONIC variants still
fail on the former. All baselines complete under the longer
windows of Traces C–E, while OrbitWeaver remains faster
by reducing checkpointing and recovery overhead.
7.3
Recovery latency
OrbitWeaver recovers quickly after resets. We use a 32K-
token request and create checkpoints at 20%, 40%, 60%, and
80% of prefill progress, with each request generating 64 to-
kens during decoding. Figure 11 reports cold-cache recovery
latency at these progress points. Across all tested devices,
models, and progress points, OrbitWeaver achieves recovery
speedups of 1.22×–6.97× over the baselines. For example,
on AGX with Qwen3-VL 4B at 20% progress, SONIC-layer,
SONIC-chunk, and HCache take 6.85×, 6.36×, and 4.40× as
long as OrbitWeaver, respectively. Even at 80% progress with
MiniCPM-V 4.5, they take 2.95×, 2.56×, and 1.50× as long,
respectively. This improvement comes from OrbitWeaver’s
dependency-aware recovery: it prioritizes the layer weights,
prefix KV cache, and hidden states that unlock useful com-
putation, defers other reads until their consumer blocks are
ready, and overlaps SSD reads with dependency-ready com-
putation. By contrast, fixed chunk-first or layer-first recovery
exposes more I/O before computation can resume.
7.4
Checkpoint overhead
OrbitWeaver runs with low normal-path overhead. Fig-
ure 12 reports uninterrupted inference latency across the
tested devices and models with prompt lengths from 2K to
32K tokens, with each request generating 64 tokens during
decoding. Part of each prompt is occupied by image tokens,
and the rest is filled with text tokens. Across all settings,
OrbitWeaver remains within 5% of the no-checkpoint ex-
ecution time while preserving recoverable progress. Com-
pared with SONIC-layer, SONIC-chunk, and HCache, Or-
bitWeaver achieves speedups of up to 2.63×, 2.16×, and 1.64×,
respectively; the corresponding geometric-mean speedups
are 1.62×, 1.38×, and 1.08×. This low normal-path overhead
comes from OrbitWeaver’s block-wise checkpointing, which
avoids persisting full-sequence hidden states after every
layer, and its storage layout, which writes the states of each
completed block as a contiguous record. Together, these de-
signs reduce device-to-host transfers and fragmented SSD
writes during inference.
7.5
Disk wear
OrbitWeaver reduces SSD writes and write amplifi-
cation. Figure 13 reports total SSD writes and DLWA for
Qwen3-VL 2B on Orin, with prompt lengths of 2K–32K
tokens and 64 generated tokens per request. Across these
lengths, SONIC-layer, SONIC-chunk, and HCache write
2.33×–3.56×, 1.08×–2.13×, and 1.10×–2.20× as much data
as OrbitWeaver, respectively. Compared with SONIC-layer,
SONIC-chunk, and HCache, OrbitWeaver reduces DLWA
by 33.6–45.4%, 14.3–46.4%, and 15.0–46.2%, respectively.
These reductions come from OrbitWeaver’s phase-aware
checkpointing, which avoids persisting redundant interme-
diate states, and its storage layout, which batches checkpoint
states into aligned, contiguous records and produces a mostly
sequential write stream. Together, these designs minimize
SSD wear under repeated checkpointing.
7.6
Energy consumption
OrbitWeaver incurs low energy overhead. Figure 14
compares uninterrupted Qwen3-VL 2B inference on Orin
with and without OrbitWeaver checkpointing, measur-
ing energy for 2K–32K prompt tokens and 64 generated
tokens per request. Across all tested prompt lengths, Or-
bitWeaver consumes only 3.75%–4.74% more energy than
the no-checkpoint baseline. This overhead comes from
persisting recoverable states during normal inference and
is consistent with the low runtime overhead in Figure 12.
The no-checkpoint baseline provides a lower bound for an
uninterrupted run but loses all in-memory progress after
a reset. OrbitWeaver therefore pays a small persistence
cost to avoid repeating completed VLM computation after
interruptions.

7.7
Case Study: Real Deployment on Sat-1 and Sat-2
OrbitWeaver sustains VLM execution across repeated
in-orbit interruptions. We deploy OrbitWeaver on Sat-1
and Sat-2 for 72 hours and execute 25 VLM requests on each
satellite. Each request runs Qwen3-VL 2B on remote-sensing
images with a 32K-token input, with each request generating
64 tokens during decoding. We impose a 20-minute timeout
on each request. On Sat-1, 21 requests experience 47 bus-
enforced shutdowns; on Sat-2, 20 requests experience 44
bus-enforced shutdowns. Across both deployments, 41 of
the 50 requests are interrupted, and OrbitWeaver completes
all 50 requests despite a total of 91 bus-enforced shutdowns.
OrbitWeaver preserves progress across bus-enforced
shutdowns. Figure 15 shows one execution on Sat-1 that
spans three execution windows and two bus-enforced shut-
downs. After each shutdown, OrbitWeaver restores the lat-
est committed checkpoint during recovery (green regions)
and resumes the unfinished request, completing it in the
third window. For comparison, Figure 15(b) shows a separate
no-checkpoint execution under repeated bus-enforced shut-
downs. Because the baseline loses all in-memory VLM states
after each shutdown, its inference progress (purple line) re-
sets to zero. It therefore repeats previously completed work
and remains in prefill after the third window. The aggregate
deployment demonstrates that OrbitWeaver repeatedly re-
covers across two satellites, while this trace illustrates how
preserving progress enables completion across interrupted
execution windows.
8
Discussion
Generalizability. OrbitWeaver primarily targets orbital
edge computing [14] to reduce reliance on ground-based pro-
cessing. Starcloud [21] and Project Suncatcher [2] envision
dedicated space-based clouds. Better power and thermal pro-
visioning may reduce interruptions, but inference progress
must still survive power cycling, resource contention, and
unexpected resets. OrbitWeaver’s checkpointing and re-
covery principles apply to these platforms, complementing
hardware co-design by letting interrupted requests resume
rather than restart.
12


--- Page 13 ---
Resuming Vision-Language Inference across Onboard Interruptions
9
Related Work
• Satellite Computing Satellite computing systems use
onboard perception and decision-making to reduce down-
link demand and response latency [5, 7, 13, 14, 18, 23, 26, 36,
40, 62, 65, 71, 74–77]. Phi-Sat-1 and Kodan reduce downlink
demand through onboard filtering [13, 26]. EagleEye cou-
ples onboard target detection with follow-up observation
scheduling across a constellation [7]. Grace and VISO adapt
VLMs to remote sensing and on-orbit execution [65, 77]. On-
satellite COTS measurements show that thermal and energy
constraints strongly shape onboard performance [70]. Or-
bitWeaver instead preserves VLM progress across resets so
long-running requests complete despite intermittent satellite
execution.
• Intermittent Computing Intermittent computing sys-
tems preserve progress across repeated power or state loss [8,
24, 32, 44, 46, 47, 49, 56, 60, 61, 64, 68]. Mementos uses check-
points on energy-harvesting devices [56]. DINO introduces
task boundaries for consistent intermittent execution [44].
Chain provides tasks and channels for intermittent execu-
tion [8]. Alpaca avoids whole-program checkpoints through
task-based privatization [46]. SONIC and Zygarde apply in-
termittent execution to embedded DNN inference [27, 30].
OrbitWeaver extends checkpointing and task-based execu-
tion to interruptions from diverse causes, windows of tens of
seconds to minutes, and multi-GiB KV and activation states
persisted to SSD/eMMC. The challenges shift to balancing
checkpoint size against preserved progress and scheduling
recovery I/O with computation.
• Efficient LLM and VLM Inference Modern VLMs com-
bine visual encoders with language models for flexible visual
reasoning and instruction following [3, 6, 10, 37, 39, 53, 55,
66]. LLM serving engines, also used as VLM backends, op-
timize continuous execution through batching, scheduling,
memory offloading, attention kernels, structured genera-
tion, prefix/KV cache reuse, and phase disaggregation [1,
11, 12, 31, 34, 48, 52, 58, 72, 79, 80]. Long-context inference
systems further reduce KV cache memory footprint or move-
ment through eviction, quantization, compression, stream-
ing, offloading, prefetching, or cache-centric disaggrega-
tion [25, 29, 35, 38, 41–43, 54, 69, 78]. Unlike these systems,
OrbitWeaver targets intermittent on-orbit inference, where
volatile activations and KV caches are lost after resets unless
they are made durable and recovered efficiently.
10
Conclusion
This paper presents OrbitWeaver, a runtime for efficient and
reliable on-satellite VLM inference through efficient check-
pointing and dynamic recovery. Evaluation demonstrates up
to 4.07× end-to-end speedup with less than 5% runtime over-
head, while in-orbit deployment confirms sustained progress
across bus-enforced shutdowns.
